article_text:
It’s interesting, to this day, how many people still don’t realize Jason Voorhees only appears for a brief second in the original “Friday the 13th” film. Spoiler for a 46-year-old film (and the opening scene of “Scream” and the entire premise of the new “ Friday the 13th ” prequel series): Jason’s mother, Pamela Voorhees, is the killer in the first film.

In the 1980 film directed by Sean S. Cunningham, we know Pamela Voorhees blames pretty much everyone at Camp Crystal Lake for the drowning death of her son, Jason Voorhees (we assume you are familiar with his work), and goes on a murderous rampage (which includes a young Kevin Bacon). The new series explores, well, how did it get to this point?

“Crystal Lake” has been in some sort of development, off and on, for around 23 years . The rights to “Friday the 13th” are mired in an extremely complicated legal situation, with different entities owning different aspects of what Jason Voorhees would become. (For example, Jason doesn’t have his iconic hockey mask until the third installment, and there are legal claims on that creation versus what we see in the first film.)

But “Crystal Lake,” with its ‘70s backdrop, is a long way off from anyone running around with a hockey mask. But! Here we are, finally , with Brad Caleb Kane getting this show made. And, now, coming off her Emmy win for “DTF St. Louis,” Linda Cardellini in the lead role of Pamela Voorhees.

Ahead, Kane and Cardellini share what each wanted from the Pamela Voorhees we see in this series, and why the show added a conspiratorial subplot that didn’t exist in the films. (Oh, and a lot of praise for Don Knotts, who we do see in the series, kind of surprisingly.)

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When Linda was cast, you didn’t realize you were getting Emmy winner Linda Cardellini.

Brad Caleb Kane: No! But she should have already had an Emmy by the time I cast her for “Crystal Lake.” But I did know that all of her performances are indelible and amazing. She has an effortless likability. One of the things I was thinking when I first reached out to Linda to talk to her about possibly taking on the part was her performance in “Dead to Me,” holding everything that she knows inside and not being able to reveal to a person what she’s done. That element of holding all of that information inside and making us see, without commenting on it, how much it’s paining her and how conflicted she is. That was a real element we needed for our Pamela Voorhees. Somebody who is keeping secrets, but you can see it is eating away inside of her. And transforms into a person that just lets her freak flag fly, joyfully. So I wanted that quality and she does it effortlessly in that show, so that’s why I reached out.

This series was first discussed as far back as 2003.

Kane: I didn’t even know that.

Sean S. Cunningham mentioned he had an idea in development. Over the years, so many people have tried. How did you do it?

Kane: Right place, right time. Right take for the right people.

And I realize this has had a very complicated legal journey.

Kane: Yeah, all that stuff is kind of above my paygrade — all the legal wrangling that went on to sort of pull all the rights together. I think that happened with A24 and Jason Inc. I think there’s another rights holder? And some people have the rights to the mask but not the name. All that stuff was done and dealt with before I came on board and pitched my take. It really was just a function of me seeing they were going to make this thing.

The great Bryan Fuller, who I am a massive fan of, had, I guess, creative differences with some of the people. And he ended up going in a different direction. But they were looking to make it with somebody because they did want to do a Pamela Voorhees prequel and, when I saw that was happening, I reached out because “Friday the 13th Part III,” it was the first “Friday the 13th” I saw in theaters.

That was 1982, right? That was my first one, but I didn’t really get into these until the pandemic. I found them comforting.

Kane: Right. And I remember a full crowd and the manipulation of that crowd and them yelling at the screen. There was a fine layer of marijuana smoke over everybody’s head with the blue beam of the projector cutting through it. It’s all very proustian for me.

And Shelly Finkelstein with his props.

Kane: Yeah, totally! Shelly Finkelstein with his props! That guy is a lawyer now. I think he’s a lawyer for some of the people who were in the various movies. Because the “Friday the 13th” universe is a small family, people reach out from other movies and stuff. And I think he’s actually a lawyer for some of those people. The actors from various movies. He’s made “Friday the 13th” representation a career.

Linda, what’s your prior relationship with “Friday the 13th”?

Linda Cardellini: I mean, I saw the movies when I was a kid. I loved scary movies when I was a kid. I think it made me seem cool, I felt like, to my older brother. I saw other ones in the theaters, but I do remember seeing “Freddy vs. Jason” in the theaters. It was in LA at Universal City Walk and it was packed . And people were screaming at the screen! I was waiting for that movie to come out. They were two icons, two worlds colliding. So I love a Halloween horror night. I mean, less so now, I’m a little bit older, but I really love the thrill and the fun of it.

And I’m a big Halloween lover. Halloween the holiday. So, all that stuff I think is really fun. I mean, you can’t really even think about the date Friday the 13th without seeing the mask in your mind, or wondering about how auspicious that date is. So I think it just worked its way in for a child of the ‘80s — it worked your way into your psyche. The same way you feel scared when you go into a pool and there might be a shark there. [ Laughs ] Because we saw “Jaws”!

Kane: To your point about finding them comforting during the pandemic, a lot of that has to do with the nostalgia factor of it and that yearning of a simpler time…

Yes, a simpler time when Jason Vorhees would run around and stab people.

Kane: But it’s a simple motive!

It was.

Kane: You step onto the camp grounds and this guy is going to get you. And probably in a very inventive and creative way.

Cardellini: And over the top.

Kane: Totally over the top. And there’s something very comforting about going back to those things of our youth that were simpler than things are now — in our personal lives or the world at large. So, yeah, that is why they are comforting in a lot of ways.

Cardellini: And it not being hyper-realistic, too, that is fun about it. That part of it makes it entertainment to digest.

Are you surprised by how many people don’t realize that Jason basically isn’t even in the first movie?

Kane: That exact thing is what got Drew Berrymore killed at the beginning of Scream. She got that answer wrong! I don’t know, do people not know now that Mrs. Voorhees was the killer in the first movie?

I think the average citizen at large does not know that.

Cardellini: And you think the hockey mask was there all along, too.

Right. Which doesn’t show up until the end of the third one.

Kane: Well, we should educate them. [ Laughs ] I like to think of myself as an educator.

Linda has a scene where she wraps a guy’s head in a clear plastic bag, who has a head wound, then the bag completely fills with blood and explodes onto your face.

Cardellini: When I read that, I was very excited. Because that’s an inventive way to see this happen. Not realizing, oh, wait a minute, I’ll be covered in that from head to toe.

Kane: Oh, you didn’t realize the reality of it on the ground?

Cardellini: No, but I thought it was so fun and inventive and strange and I love that about parts of the show. We took a week to shoot that sequence. Is it like a 15-minute sequence?

Kane: It’s like a 20-minute sequence.

Cardellini: It’s a 20-minute sequence and there’s not very much talking.

Kane: There’s virtually no talking.

Cardellini: And she’s just being put through it physically. To me, I loved that about it. That it wasn’t dialogue-heavy and that it was really about … ah … that it was cinematic to me. It read cinematic to me and I thought that would be a lot of fun and I hadn’t done anything like that before. After, I think that is such a great tableau for her, looking in the mirror, “What did you do?” And being at that point in her life, it sets you on the road for what you’re about to see. And how does she become that person.

Kane: And all of that stuff is just a function of her trying to survive. None of that is gratuitous, “Oh, let’s show you a whole bunch of blood.” She was trying to survive. She does what she does…

Cardellini: She’s trying to clean it up!

Kane: She’s trying to clean it up and not turn it into this mess and it turns into this thing. It’s the escalating situations of growing absurdity.

And we feel a lot of empathy for Jason in the flashbacks and how he’s treated, I never thought I’d say that sentence.

Kane: I’m one of those people who believes, concretely, that monsters are not born. They are made. There might be some genetic predisposition or some chemical thing that may be going on, then turned on. I wanted to show that monsters like Jason and Pamela were not monsters to begin with. They were formed by certain circumstances and situations and manipulations.

We come to TV for character. We want to spend time with characters. We want to get to know them and we want to empathize with them. And, obviously, Jason and Pamala Voorhees are our main characters in this franchise. So how do you empathize with them? Well, you have to show them as human beings.

There’s a conspiratorial aspect and mystery to this show that isn’t really present in the films…

Kane: We set the show in the ‘70s, because the first movie was 1980…

Right, Pamela Voorhees is watching Don Knotts on TV.

Kane: Don Knotts! Yes! The Don Knotts variety show. I’m a big “The Ghost and Mr. Chicken” fan. Legitimately, not ironically.

Not “The Incredible Mr. Limpet”?

Kane: I like “The Incredible Mr. Limpet,” but seeing Don Knotts’ voice come out of that fish is not as exciting.

I was big into “The Apple Dumpling Gang.”

Kane: I grew up on that. Well, now we’re just talking Don Knotts…

Cardellini: I love Don Knotts.

Kane: But, if you’re going to set something in the ‘70s, specifically, what was so prominent that decade — the movies that were prominent and the feeling that was in the air. For America, the feeling in the ‘70s that was really prominent was mistrust in institutions. You see that in the movies that are really popular at the time, specifically the Alan Pakula paranoid thrillers trilogy. “Klute,” “The Parallax View,” “All the President’s Men.” Even movies like “Three Days of the Condor.” So it felt like, if we are going to do a show that takes place in the ‘70s, let’s bring that aspect to it. Let’s have Pamela and Jason be on the run from something and have it parallel the things that were going on in America at the time.

There’s been a lot of speculation I’ve seen online, “Oh, is he making Jason a supersoldier?” “Is this a ‘Stranger Things’?” “Is this ‘Jason XI’?” It’s none of that. It’s nothing that’s out of the realm of reality. It’s all stuff that’s based in science and things that were going on at the time. He’s not a genetically engineered anything. That conspiracy that we learn about later in the season comes out of a very specific human instinct that Pamela has, that’s been turned on its head and turned into manipulation and gaslighting and all the things that women and America had to go through at this time in American history.

I’m going to embarrass Linda now, but we had what we had on the page, and I say this legitimately, the show doesn’t work unless you have an actor who approaches this character seriously and with respect. And the spirit of creating a real situation under these imaginary circumstances. And she came to work and she put in the thought behind it…

And in her last show, she singlehandedly brought back the phrase, “No way, Jose.”

Kane: [ Laughs ] I love that.

Cardellini: [ Laughs ] I’ll take it!

All eight episodes of “Crystal Lake” start streaming on Peacock on Thursday, October 15.
excerpt_original: Star Cardellini and showrunner Brad Caleb Kane scare up a hell of a good "Friday the 13th" prequel. They tell IndieWire how '70s paranoia, their own horror proclivities, and Don Knotts (yes, Don Knotts) turn the story of Pamela Voorhees into something truly juicy.

editorial_title_zh: 工匠们在萨凡纳 SCAD 电影节上剖析木马设计的妙招与巧思
editorial_excerpt_zh: 制片设计师鲁思·德·容、剪辑师莎拉·布罗沙以及服装设计师艾米·罗斯向 IndieWire 讲述了他们各自在创作中融入的隐秘巧思。

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "布罗沙能够让自己和审片的其他人感到惊喜的方式之一就是声音，特别是对于像《Disclosure Day》火车追逐戏那样妙趣横生的动作场面。“和任何事情一样，这只需要耐心和想象力，你要关注事情的节奏——你希望在何时何地看到火车、它有多远、我们什么时候听到火车的动静、声音有多大？”布罗沙说。“我有很棒的助理，他们做了非常棒的声音工作，我只是不断要求他们做得更多。他们会说：‘我们在这上面花了3天时间。’而我会说：‘太好了。现在再花3天。’然后我们就继续做得更多、更多、更多、更多。接着，你知道的，一旦伟大的加里·雷德斯特罗姆（Gary Rydstrom）、布莱恩·乔米尔（Bryan Chomier）和他们的团队带着音效介入，一切就都会被打磨完美。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "无论是声音、色彩还是自然元素本身，正是工匠们在作品中融入的惊艳细节和点睛之笔，才让电影制作的每一个部门都充满生机。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival , IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026. On the artisans panel, “ The Odyssey ” production designer Ruth de Jong , “Paper Tiger” and “ I Play Rocky ” costume designer Amy Roth, and “ Disclosure Day ” editor Sarah Broshar spoke to students and guests about their process and approaches towards each of their particular corners of the giant puzzle that is putting a film together.

But there was one thing that united all of them, across their different creative disciplines, and that was the importance of (sometimes quite literally) climbing hilltops to create a sense of authentic surprise.

If a costume designer can delight a director without being asked for something specific, then the movie is alive. If the editor’s intuitive sense of rhythm is working in harmony with the footage that’s been shot, then in a lot of respects the film is showing the post team what it wants to be. And if a production designer can build a Trojan Horse to the right scale and it falls down? Well, don’t panic. It can look even more weathered and accurate to the initial plan when it’s picked back up again.

“Obviously the scale [of the horse] came from me needing to fill it physically with the actors and the IMAX camera and [cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema] and Chris. So that’s how we proportionally worked out and built several of them, then built a separate body of the horse to physically shoot that scene, lowered it into a tank, and shot that on a set near our city of Troy,” De Jong said.

But in addition to needing to half-drown Odysseus (Matt Damon) and his companions, an IMAX camera, cinematographer, and acclaimed director, some of the aspects that make the Trojan Horse truly look like it’s been in the wars came about organically.

“[For the opening], we mounted the horse to a massive trench plate and got a dredger. We dredged up really deep into the sand. We did a few tests a couple of days before. We put the horse in the waves. It took a beating. It fell. We had to rebuild it overnight to then shoot the next day. So the horse you are seeing in the film went through a lot before it got shot. It was very physical,” De Jong said. “Water always wins.”

But according to De Jong, the work of production design, even on projects without the grand scope of “ The Odyssey ,” is always the same. “ I feel deeply that if my sets are too obvious, I’ve failed because they should fade to the back and the actors should just be immersed in their worlds, and the audience should be lost in that world,” De Jong said.

This is as much the case for good contemporary costume design, where the clothes should just help us make judgments about the characters and feel the shifts in the story, something Amy Roth talked about doing almost invisibly in both “I Play Rocky” and “Paper Tiger.” With the former, Roth took a lot of cues not just from the existing material around “Rocky” and Sylvester Stallone, but about how the character of ‘Mike’ would feel about his body as he worked himself up into becoming Sly.

“He really was like three people,” Roth said. “Dressing him early on was taking hints from a future Sly and putting them in the way he dresses so that we can see the impetus of how ‘Rocky’ came to be. He was big into working out and he was very body conscious. So that silhouette was important to me and I was literally, like, layering clothing onto Anthony so that he couldn’t bulk up,” Roth said.

Meanwhile on “Paper Tiger,” Roth worked in a silent partnership with the sets in order to give the characters caught up in a mob scheme more or less agency. “The house was very beige, so I put the actors just so that the mother was in focus. And then in the end she starts to fade. She starts sort of matching the walls; the mother and father sort of fade into the background. And that’s just me doing my thing. I don’t think I even discussed that with James [Grey, the director], but he would’ve liked it.”

What the director likes and how the director is responding gets very important in the edit, which is where Broshar’s developed a great read on Steven Spielberg over the course of their many collaborations.

“When you’re spending hours and weeks and months and years sitting in a room with somebody, you get shorthands. You don’t have to say words as much. You can just kind of feel a twitch. If I make a little twitch, Steven will look at me, like, ‘What? What are you thinking?’ You can tell,” Broshar said. “I think you’re just always trying to sit down and watch the movie or watch the scene like you’ve never seen it before. I always watch myself watching something, and I try to see if I’m feeling tense or if I am getting distracted or thinking about what’s for lunch — and that is a real red flag.”

One of the ways in which Broshar can help surprise herself and the other folks watching a cut is with sound, especially on a delightfully bonkers action sequence like “Disclosure Day” has in its train chase. “Like anything, it just takes patience and imagination, and you keep an eye on the timing of things — where and how do you want to see the train, how far away is it, when do we hear the train, how loud is it?” Broshar said. “ I have great assistants who do really good sound work, and I just kept asking them for more. They’d say, ‘We spent three days on this.’ And I’m like, ‘Great. Now spend three more.’ And let’s just keep [going] more, more, more, more. And then, you know, it all gets polished out as soon as great Gary Rydstrom and Bryan Chomier and their team come in with sound.”

Whether it’s sound, color, or the elements of nature themselves, it’s the surprises and flourishes that artisans build into their work that help each filmmaking department feel alive.

article_text:
Juno Temple (“Ted Lasso,” “Fargo”), Joey King (“We Were the Lucky Ones,” “The Act”) and James McAvoy (“The Last King of Scotland,” “Atonement”) are set to star in the upcoming — and somewhat timely — sci-fi AI comedy movie “Almost You.”

The film, currently shooting in Glasgow, is being directed by Matt Lipsey, whose credits include multiple episodes of the Emmy-winning “Ted Lasso” as well as “Inside No. 9” and “Little Britain.”

Related Stories

Bill Burr on ‘The Social Reckoning,’ Sparring With Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg and Why Tech CEOs are ‘Leading Us to Ruin’

Bankside Films has acquired the feature for worldwide sales and is co-repping for the U.K. and North America with UTA Independent Film Group.

Popular on Variety

“Almost You” follows Phoebe, a brilliant robotics engineer struggling to come to terms with the death of her younger sister, Edie. Defying all the protocols of the tech company she works for, Phoebe uses years of messages, videos and social media posts to create a lifelike AI replica of her sister, at first bringing her a great deal of joy and comfort. However, as per the synopsis. Phoebe’s extraordinary invention soon forces her to confront one impossible question: if you could bring someone back, should you?

“Almost You” reunites McAvoy with Danny Page, who produced his directorial debut “California Schemin’,” which recently released in the U.S., and his latest feature “Faith,” which debuted in Toronto. Page produces for Homefront Productions and Blazing Griffin alongside Matt Schichter (“Mother Father Sister Brother Frank,” “CFNY: The Spirit of Radio”) of Scared Goose Entertainment and Rory Stewart. the film is being produced in association with Parker Films (James McAvoy and Lisa Liberati) with financing by Blazing Griffin and Homefront Productions. Finance is also being provided by Yeti Entertainment and Head Gear Films.

“There’s never been a movie that needed to be made more than this one,” said Lipsey. “We thought we were making a film about the future. It turns out it’s about right now. Juno, Joey and James will make you laugh, then break your heart, then make you laugh about it.”

Adde Stephen Kelliher of Bankside Films said: “We are incredibly excited to be working with Matt Lipsey and this exceptional cast on ‘Almost You.’ Combining a wonderfully original premise with genuine emotional depth and humour, the film explores the very human desire to hold on to the people we love, in a world where technology increasingly challenges the boundaries of what is possible. It is a funny, moving and thought-provoking story which we believe will resonate strongly with audiences around the world.”

Matt Lipsey is repped by Curtis Brown Group, Juno Temple is repped by UTA, Maison 2, B-Side, Relevant and Lichter, Grossman; Joey King is repped by WME, Brillstein, The Lede Company and Hirsch Wallerstein; and James McAvoy is repped by United Agents, UTA, The Lede Company and Sloane Offer.

article_text:
Jogo vendeu mais de 40 milhões de cópias em todo o mundo.

A Paramount está desenvolvendo um filme em live-action ambientado no mundo de “ Cyberpunk 2077 “, um dos jogos de ação mais vendidos dos últimos anos. O produtor Lorenzo di Bonaventura está vinculado ao projeto junto à CD Projekt Red , a premiada desenvolvedora de videogames sediada na Polônia e detentora dos direitos da franquia (via Deadline ).

O jogo se passa na metrópole cyberpunk fictícia de Night City, na Califórnia, dentro do universo distópico de “Cyberpunk”. No centro da trama está V, um mercenário que, relutantemente, recebe um “biochip” cibernético contendo o engrama do lendário astro do rock e terrorista Johnny Silverhand. À medida que a consciência de Silverhand começa a sobrescrever a de V, ambos precisam trabalhar juntos para se separarem e salvarem a vida de V, enfrentando a Corporação Arasaka — uma poderosa megacorporação que atua como a governante de fato da cidade.

“Cyberpunk” começou como um jogo de RPG criado por Mike Pondsmith no final dos anos 1980, tendo desde então se expandido em diversas frentes. “Cyberpunk 2077” vendeu mais de 40 milhões de cópias em todo o mundo, enquanto sua expansão, “Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty”, vendeu 15 milhões de cópias. Na Netflix, o anime “Cyberpunk: Edgerunners” é também sucesso de audiência.

Ainda não há previsão de estreia para o filme em live-action de “Cyberpunk 2077”.

article_text:
Entrano nel vivo i preparativi per la prima edizione autunnale di Popsophia a Pesaro, in programma dal 5 al 7 novembre 2026 e dedicata quest’anno al tema Contrasti . Da lunedì, 26 ottobre, alle ore 14, apriranno le prenotazioni per i philoshow serali all’Auditorium Scavolini e per la mostra In-possibile a Palazzo Gradari, entrambi a ingresso gratuito.

Il festival si svilupperà in tre sedi della città: il Centro Arti Visive Pescheria ospiterà gli incontri pomeridiani, Palazzo Gradari le attività a partire dalle 16:30, mentre l’Auditorium Scavolini accoglierà i philoshow serali dalle 21:15.

Si tratta della prima edizione autunnale del festival diretto da Lucrezia Ercoli e nasce come una sorta di “secondo tempo” della programmazione estiva, con l’obiettivo di consolidare la presenza di Popsophia nel calendario culturale cittadino anche oltre i mesi tradizionalmente legati ai grandi eventi.

Il punto di partenza è l’idea che differenze e ambivalenze non debbano per forza trasformarsi in scontro, ma possano diventare strumenti per leggere il presente. «L’idea che alberga nelle giornate di novembre è che può esistere un modo di ragionare che si discosta dalla modalità del talk show televisivo», spiega Ercoli. «I nostri contrasti tengono insieme le contraddizioni e le ambivalenze che fanno parte dell’esistenza di ciascuno di noi».

Anche l’immagine scelta per il festival traduce visivamente questa impostazione: un volto bifronte, giovane e vecchio, ricavato da una scultura identificata probabilmente con un Ermes propileo attribuito ad Alcamene. Due profili rivolti in direzioni opposte condividono lo stesso corpo, trasformandosi nell’emblema della manifestazione.

Due philoshow per Bob Dylan e Freddie Mercury

Le prenotazioni riguarderanno in particolare le due serate filosofico-musicali del 6 e 7 novembre. Il primo appuntamento sarà Like a Rolling Stone, le parole di Bob Dylan , in programma venerdì 6 novembre alle 21:15. Sabato 7 novembre, alla stessa ora, sarà invece la volta di Somebody to Love, filosofia di Freddie Mercury .

I posti potranno essere riservati gratuitamente attraverso il sito ufficiale di Popsophia, accedendo al collegamento Eventbrite. Il biglietto garantirà l’ingresso fino a 15 minuti prima dell’inizio dello spettacolo; oltre quel termine, in assenza di check-in, il posto potrà essere riassegnato fino al raggiungimento della capienza massima.

Dal 26 ottobre sarà possibile prenotare anche l’accesso alla mostra In-possibile , visitabile a Palazzo Gradari nei pomeriggi di venerdì 6 e sabato 7 novembre a partire dalle 16:30. Il percorso prevede anche l’utilizzo di visori VR, inserendo così la dimensione immersiva all’interno del programma dedicato ai Contrasti .

Ingresso libero per gli appuntamenti pomeridiani

Non sarà invece necessaria alcuna prenotazione per gli incontri pomeridiani ospitati al Centro Arti Visive Pescheria e per la serata inaugurale di giovedì 5 novembre. La tre giorni pesarese inaugura così una nuova formula autunnale per Popsophia, che affiancherà riflessione filosofica, musica, immagini e tecnologie immersive, distribuendo gli appuntamenti tra diversi luoghi culturali della città.

article_text:
Streaming superstar IShowSpeed has partnered with Breakwater Studios and Barack and Michelle Obama’s Higher Ground to bring Ben Proudfoot’s upcoming documentary “ The Eyes of Ghana ” to theaters for a one-night-only screening on Oct. 28, Variety can reveal exclusively. Participating exhibitors include Regal, AMC, Cinemark, select theater chains and independent cinemas.

“The Eyes of Ghana,” which premiered at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival , follows Ghanaian cinematographer Chris Hesse, who, as his eyesight declines, attempts to rescue more than 1,000 films capturing Africa’s fight for independence in the 1950s and ’60s. The tapes were hidden for decades after the 1996 overthrow of Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana’s first president and a leader of the African liberation movement.

“It is a great honor to be part of ‘The Eyes of Ghana’ and help bring this extraordinary piece of history to the big screen. I felt a profound connection to Ghana when I visited this year, and learning about Chris Hesse’s work deepened my understanding of the country and its people,” said IShowSpeed. “His camera captured the birth of African independence, and his determination to preserve those images has ensured that future generations can witness it for themselves. I’m humbled by his legacy and proud to help bring his story to my community.”

IShowSpeed, who’s real name is Darren Watkins Jr., is a Cincinnati native with more than 200 million followers and subscribers across streaming and social media platforms. Known for his high-energy demeanor, his livestream content covers gaming, sports, stunts and travel. He was named to the inaugural TIME100 Creators list and ranked No. 1 on Rolling Stone’s 2025 Most Influential Creators list.

IShowSpeed’s involvement in “The Eyes of Ghana” is just the latest example of digital creators mobilizing their audiences to movie theaters. Back in January, YouTuber Mark Fischbach, aka Markiplier, directed, starred in and self-distributed his sci-fi horror film “Iron Lung.” Not only did his fans call theater chains to encourage them to screen the movie, but they also showed out in droves on release day. The film opened to $17 million and ended its run with $50 million worldwide against a budget of just $3 million.

“Chris Hesse spent more than six decades documenting and safeguarding an extraordinary chapter of Ghanaian and African history,” stated Ethan Lewis, head of non-fiction at Higher Ground. “Higher Ground is proud to partner with IShowSpeed, Ben Proudfoot and Breakwater Studios and this accomplished team of artists to bring this remarkable story to theaters on Oct. 28th. ‘The Eyes of Ghana’ speaks to the power of film to preserve our collective memory, and to the responsibility we share in making sure these stories reach the next generation.”

In addition to IShowSpeed, the film is produced by Proudfoot, Nana Adwoa Frimpong, Moses Bwayo, Anita Afonu, Brandon Somerhalder, Lewis and Vinnie Malhotra. Executive producers include Barack and Michelle Obama, Sir John Akomfrah, Kofi Amoo-Gottfried, Paula Madison, Dan and Lian Gill, Max Johnson, Jonathan E. Lim, Michael Risley, Josh Rosenberg, David Treatman and Esther Wojcicki.

Tickets and local showtimes are available at TheEyesOfGhana.com. Check out the trailer below.

article_text:
A leading light of China’s new photography, Hailun Ma, whose work slips between personal projects and fashion commissions, brings her first major solo exhibition abroad, “Hometown,” to Foam in Amsterdam, and carries us off to Xinjiang.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Hailun Ma .

“The air always smells of dust,” Ma writes of her native land. Born in 1992 in Ürümqi, the capital of Xinjiang, on China’s far northwestern edge, and a member of the country’s Han majority, she grew up in a city where Uyghurs, Kazakhs, and many other peoples brush shoulders. In high school, she borrowed her parents’ digital camera to take her first pictures. The imagery of her homeland has fed her ever since, as these lines about summers spent with her father attest: “Poplar trees, narrow irrigation ditches, sheep under the apple trees. Donkey carts, livestock bazaars.”

In 2013, she left to study photography and fashion imagery at the School of Visual Arts in New York. In Brooklyn, where everyone wears their roots with swagger, she began to see the city of her childhood in a new light. “I want to show the cool side of Xinjiang, a side I’m calling Uruklyn,” she said. The portmanteau, a contraction of Ürümqi and Brooklyn, gave rise to a project launched in 2021: residents of Ürümqi and Kashgar, an oasis city in the region’s southwest, strike poses on their rooftops and street corners, just as New York hipsters might. Kashgar is also the birthplace of the series “Kashi Youth,” in which a 2025 image shows a helmeted young woman in leopard print, pink tulle ruffles, and white sneakers, standing before a motorcycle draped in red lace like a fashion accessory.

Far from the images of surveillance and repression that dominate media coverage of Xinjiang, Ma turns her gaze to the everyday lives of its people. Through her lens, the young revive their parents’ traditions by running them through the filter of global urban culture. Within a single frame, an embroidered skullcap crowns a baseball cap, and sneakers tread on traditional rugs. Weaned on basketball and hip-hop, Ma’s generation saw Nike as a window onto the world, and the American brand is everywhere: “They’re not barefoot. They’re wearing the latest Dunks and Jordans,” the photographer notes.

Her eye lingers on details. Hometown (2018) isolates a smile that bares a gleaming set of braces. In Xinjiang Fashion Guide (2019), henna-stained fingers tuck banknotes beneath sheer tights, just above a hot-pink lace stocking. The frame also opens onto the Pamir Mountains, where Love in Tashkurgan (2025) shows women and children in embroidered pillbox hats, perched proudly in the bed of a pickup truck. The exhibition’s curator, Aya Musa, sums up what is at play in these images: “A color can hold a memory. A pose can hold a wish. A garment can hold a route between generations.”

Hailun Ma’s “Hometown” is on view through January 20, 2027, at Foam in Amsterdam, the Netherlands.

article_text:
Ce film-là n’est pas flou. On avait laissé Hong Sang-soo sur In Water (2024), où le point jamais fait à l’image donnait aux paysages des couleurs délavées, rappelant les œuvres de Mark Rothko ; et Ce que cette nature te dit (2025), qui jouait aussi d’une photographie nébuleuse. Ici, l’image est en noir et blanc, nette, et le cadre tellement fixe dans un premier temps que l’on se demande s’il s’agit d’une nouvelle performance formelle. Presque. Le réalisateur sud-coréen utilise ici la répétition : trois jeunes journalistes se succèdent pour interviewer Bae Jeongsu, une actrice sur le retour.

Elle vient de tourner dans un film d’auteur et répond différemment à chacun en fonction de microévénements de contexte – accepter une bière en plein milieu de l’après-midi peut tout changer. Plus tard, lors d’un cours de théâtre, l’actrice tente de rejouer ces entrevues pour mieux les revisiter… On pense à Hotel by the River (2018), à ce Hong Sang-soo qu’on aime, architecte de la parole qu’on a connu plus filou. Ce film aussi se tient bien, sans prétention dans sa réflexion sur la nature des échanges professionnels. Il y a bien quelques piques sur les journalistes, mais ce n’est pas un pamphlet satirique, et l’écriture ne rate pas le personnage de l’actrice non plus. Le film lui rend plutôt un hommage, et offre un dialogue réussi sur les choix et les chemins de vie.

Le Jour de son retour de Hong Sang-soo , Carlotta Films (1 h 24) sortie le 14 octobre

article_text:
Antonin Baudry ’s two-part World War II epic about Charles de Gaulle made its U.S. premiere Saturday at the American French Film Festival in Los Angeles, drawing a seven-minute standing ovation after both installments, each running more than two and a half hours, played back-to-back to packed audiences at the DGA Theater.

The €74 million production, starring Simon Abkarian as the French general and Simon Russell Beale as Winston Churchill, marks one of Pathé ’s boldest gambles following “The Count of Monte Cristo” and the two-part “The Three Musketeers,” which were also distributed in the U.S. by Samuel Goldwyn Films.

Related Stories

Fox Closes $22 Billion Roku Takeover, Says Streaming Platform Will Remain 'Open Ecosystem'

How to Watch MLB World Series 2026: Tampa Bay Rays vs. Milwaukee Brewers Online for Free

After a slow start in France, the films quietly gained momentum through word of mouth, becoming a domestic box office success and selling over six million tickets, and are now gaining traction internationally. In the U.K., the first installment, “De Gaulle: Resistance,” which charts De Gaulle’s heroic battle to build a Resistance movement after France surrendered to Nazi Germany in 1940, currently ranks as the highest-grossing French-language film of the year. “De Gaulle” has also just been acquired in China – a rare feat — where Light Films will release it in late November.

In the U.S., Goldwyn is rolling out the epic theatrically across major U.S. markets, including New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, San Francisco, Washington, D.C., Seattle, Austin, Minneapolis, Houston and Atlanta, while making it available nationwide on transactional VOD. The second film, “De Gaulle: Liberty” will be released in early December.

Speaking to Variety during the American French Film Festival, Peter Goldwyn said he’s betting that the sprawling saga can appeal to U.S. audiences even if it revolves around a French historical figure that many aren’t familiar with.

“The films have proven themselves, and audiences are audiences, whether they’re American or French,” Goldwyn said. “It’s an amazing feat of filmmaking that you don’t quite see anymore and ultimately, World War II is an easy entry point for U.S. audiences.”

“U.S. audiences have been very much enthusiastic consistently about stories about Roosevelt, about Churchill, and I think that the story of De Gaulle is relatively untold in America,” he continued, adding that the “staggering scope and scale of what (De Gaulle) accomplished as one man is pretty amazing.”

Goldwyn argued that the films’ cinematic ambition places them closer to Hollywood blockbusters than conventional European arthouse fare.

“As a film itself, you’re looking at something on the scale of ‘The Odyssey.’ It’s just really broad and massive, and yet instead of getting lost in the effects and the war itself, it really does come down to a character study which drives the story along. So you’re not just sitting there watching World War II play out,” he said.

“The only thing that makes it an arthouse movie is because it’s in a foreign language,” he added, pointing out that the French language “makes it hard for theaters to commit on that wide of a screen count.”

As such, Goldwyn opted to pair the theatrical run with a nationwide transactional VOD release, giving the films the best chance of finding their audience.

“In France it had this sort of slow start and was really discovered, but theaters in the U.S. don’t have the patience or time to let things be discovered. It’s sort of you’re in and you’re out,” he said. “So it’s a combination method.”

The distributor is mounting a single campaign for both installments, targeting not only arthouse moviegoers but also history buffs, schools, cultural institutions and younger audiences through social media. “I think it’s enhancement, especially when you have two movies of this length, you need word of mouth and if you can only have a couple showtimes a day, you can only get so many people into the theaters,” Goldwyn said.

The appeal of the films also lies in the fact that they challenge the familiar American and British narratives of World War II, exposing the tensions between De Gaulle, Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt, played by Campbell Scott.

Baudry and his co-screenwriter, Bérénice Vila, read more than 150 books and dug into historical archives to reconstruct the general’s extraordinary journey from an isolated, virtually unknown military officer in 1940 to the leader of the French Resistance, as well as his relationship with Churchill and Roosevelt.

“They had different conceptions of war. Roosevelt, for his part, thought Churchill was being completely absurd with his romantic ideas about supporting this admirable little leader called De Gaulle. To Roosevelt, the idea of Free France was a little fantasy of Churchill’s,” said Baudry.

The director said the complicated relationship among the three leaders remains largely unknown outside academic circles.

“All of this history has never really been told. Historians, real historians who research this period and have access to the sources, know all of this, but the general public doesn’t. And the version of history taught in schools is not very complete,” he said.

Despite the historical complexity, Baudry wanted the films to be accessible to viewers with no knowledge of De Gaulle, so he organized early screenings for young students outside academic circles.

“My goal was that you could watch the film without any outside references, without ever having heard of that period or of De Gaulle,” he said.

One of Baudry’s boldest choices was casting Abkarian, a renowned actor with a career in film and theater who isn’t a bankable star, to embody the towering historical figure.

Abkarian spent roughly six months preparing for the role of De Gaulle, whose rigid posture, distinctive voice and almost eccentric behavior have long made him difficult to portray.

“I read the screenplay more than ten times. I read it and reread it and annotated things,” Abkarian told Variety. “There was nothing to change in the writing, not even a comma. The dialogue was really well written.”

The iconic monologues came more naturally. “There were the great speeches, and that’s where I feel at home because I come from the theater and I know how to approach them.”

Abkarian also transcribed every line of his dialogue into a small notebook that he carried throughout the 150-day shoot and eventually gave to Baudry.

“All the dialogue went right up to the very last page. I hadn’t planned it that way, but every page was filled. I didn’t have to use another notebook,” he said.

But the actor eventually abandoned the idea of simply reproducing De Gaulle’s mannerisms. “You can’t represent a character like this in a strictly anthropological way. You can invoke him, evoke him, but you can’t actually become him. And it wouldn’t make sense to try,” he said.

One breakthrough came when Abkarian and Baudry spent an evening recording De Gaulle’s speeches together.

“We explored how far I could go in approaching his voice, its frequency, its musicality and the way he emphasized certain words that wouldn’t naturally occur to you. I had to understand his logic, the way he articulated his thoughts through language,” Abkarian said. “I couldn’t make him speak in the ordinary, conversational way I’m speaking to you now. Between doing nothing and caricature, I had to find the right balance.”

The screenplay portrays Churchill and De Gaulle as unlikely allies bound by mutual admiration despite their frequent clashes, and Abkarian found an easy partner in Russell Beale.

“Simon is an incredible actor who has a profound understanding of great texts, and we have the same approach to the craft,” Abkarian said. “The writing provides such rich material for the actors, particularly for De Gaulle and Churchill.”

For Abkarian, Churchill and De Gaulle were united by an idealism that set them apart from Roosevelt’s political pragmatism.

“Churchill and De Gaulle were romantics. They recognized that quality in each other. That’s why they developed that friendship,” he said. “And that’s what makes their relationship beautiful, as well as mad and contradictory.”

Abkarian is less certain than Goldwyn about how Americans will respond to the films’ portrayal of their wartime leadership, but he believes De Gaulle’s defiance could strike a chord, particularly in today’s political climate.

“There may be something in De Gaulle’s struggle that speaks to Americans’ own battles, to their sense of nobility and their democratic convictions,” he said. “I think that, from that point of view, Americans could recognize themselves in the Gaullist struggle.”

Goldwyn, for his part, sees a hero Americans will recognize. “It’s a story of an ally,” Goldwyn said. “This man was very patriotic, which I think is very American. He didn’t go along with what his government dictated and said, ‘I don’t believe this, I need to fight for my country.’”
